oneSentence: An AI system offered under terms that keep key parts, such as model weights, training details or code, under the provider’s control rather than openly shared.
plainExplanation:
A proprietary model is an AI model that people can use only under conditions set by the organisation that built or sells it. The provider may let users send prompts or data in and receive outputs back, but it does not fully share how the system was built. Important parts may stay private, such as the model weights, which are the numerical settings learned during training, the training data, the code, or the licence terms.

What goes in depends on the service. A user might enter text, an image or audio. The provider’s system processes that input on its own infrastructure or in software it controls. What comes out is a prediction, classification, translation, summary, image or other result. The user sees the output, but often cannot inspect or modify the internal model in detail.

This term is often confused with open-source AI and open-weight models. They are not the same. A model can have open weights but still keep some training data, code or usage rights restricted. A proprietary model usually keeps more control with the provider, especially over access, copying, redistribution and inspection.

For leaders and policy staff, the key question is not only performance. It is also governance. Who can audit the system? Who can host it? What can be checked after an error? What happens if the provider changes the terms, prices or safety features? Those practical limits are often the real meaning of "proprietary" in use.

everydayAnalogy.title: Using a sealed translation booth
everydayAnalogy.story: At an international meeting, a company provides a translation booth with skilled staff inside. Delegates speak into a microphone and hear translated audio through headsets. The service works, but the company does not allow anyone to enter the booth, inspect the notes, copy the method or hire another team to run the same setup. If the company changes its price or rules, the meeting organisers must accept that or switch services.

everydayAnalogy.limitation: A human translation team can explain parts of its method, adapt intentionally and be directly supervised in real time. A proprietary AI model is software, usually operating through learned numerical parameters rather than human judgement. Also, some proprietary models can be run locally under contract, while the sealed-booth story suggests one fixed service setup.

visual.title: Proprietary model: what the user gets and what stays with the provider
visual.learningObjective: After viewing this, the reader should be able to say that a proprietary model may allow use of outputs without giving open access to weights, code, training details or redistribution rights.
visual.description: A two-column comparison. The left column shows what a user can usually access: input box, API or app, and outputs. The right column shows what often remains under provider control: weights, code, training data details, hosting choices and licence terms. Read from top to bottom to see the boundary between use and control.

steps.label: What the user sends
steps.explanation: The user provides a prompt, document, image or other input through an app, website or application programming interface, often called an API.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a user icon on the left with arrows to three small input boxes labelled text, image and audio, feeding into a box labelled service interface.

steps.label: What the provider’s system does
steps.explanation: The provider runs the model and related software on systems it controls, or under tightly controlled terms if customers can deploy it.
steps.visualInstruction: Place a central processing box between columns, shaded to show provider control, with sublabels model runtime and safety filters.

steps.label: What the user receives
steps.explanation: The user gets an output such as a summary, translation, score or generated image, but not necessarily the internal model itself.
steps.visualInstruction: From the central box, draw arrows back to the left toward output cards labelled summary, translation and score.

steps.label: What stays closed
steps.explanation: Key parts may remain unavailable for inspection, copying or modification, including weights, source code, training data information and redistribution rights.
steps.visualInstruction: On the right, stack locked boxes labelled weights, code, training details, hosting control and licence restrictions, each connected to the central processing box.

visual.interaction: Hovering or tapping each locked box reveals a short note on what that restriction can limit, such as auditing, portability or independent hosting.
visual.accessibilityDescription: This comparison diagram explains that a proprietary model separates use from control. On the left, a user sends text, image or audio through an app or API and receives outputs such as summaries, translations or scores. In the centre, the provider runs the model and related safety systems. On the right, several locked boxes show parts that often remain under provider control: model weights, source code, training data details, hosting choices and licence rights. The main point is that users may access the service without gaining full access to the internal model or the right to copy and redistribute it.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: A static two-column layout shows accessible user-facing features on the left and provider-controlled internal components on the right, with labels instead of hover effects.

workedExample.scenario: A regional business wants an AI tool to help staff resolve ambiguous pronouns in customer emails, such as deciding whether "she" refers to Amina or Sofia in a message thread.
workedExample.input: Email text: "Amina called Sofia after the shipment arrived. She said the boxes were damaged."
process: Staff send the sentence to a commercial language model through an API.
The provider’s service processes the text using its own model weights and system settings, which the business cannot inspect fully.
The service returns an answer such as: "'She' is ambiguous here; it could refer to Amina or Sofia."
The business can use the output in its workflow, but it cannot retrain that exact model itself, examine all training sources or redistribute the model to another vendor.
workedExample.result: The organisation gains a useful language output, but remains dependent on the provider for access, updates, pricing and many audit details.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: A UN office is considering a commercial AI service to translate non-sensitive field updates into a working language for faster internal triage.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: Whether the model is proprietary affects procurement, oversight, auditability, hosting options, vendor dependence and what evidence the office can obtain about performance and safeguards.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: Do not paste confidential, personal, protection-sensitive, security-sensitive or operational information into an unapproved public AI service; use only approved channels and keep human review over any translated output.

whyItMatters: For decision-makers, "proprietary" signals a governance choice, not just a technical one. It affects procurement, cost, bargaining power, audit access, security review, data handling, business continuity and exit options if a supplier changes terms or stops a service. It also affects accountability after harm or error. If important parts are closed, an organisation may have less ability to inspect how the system was built, test it independently, reproduce results or move the workload elsewhere. That does not make proprietary models automatically bad or unsafe, and open models are not automatically better. It means the trade-offs must be examined clearly before adoption.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A proprietary model is simply a model you have to pay for.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Price and openness are different questions. Some paid services share more technical access than others, and some free services still keep weights, code and training details closed. The core issue is control over inspection, modification, hosting and redistribution, not only whether there is a fee.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Proprietary means the model is better or safer than open alternatives.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Closed access does not by itself prove higher quality or stronger safety. A proprietary provider may invest heavily in testing and safeguards, but outside scrutiny can also be limited. Quality and safety need evidence from evaluation, governance and suitable use, not assumptions based on business model alone.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If an API is available, the model is open.
commonMisconceptions.correction: An API lets people use a service interface. It does not usually grant access to the underlying weights, source code, training data details or redistribution rights. You may be able to send inputs and receive outputs while the most important internal parts remain closed.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: A proprietary model is an AI service you can use, but the company keeps important parts under its control instead of sharing them openly.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: In technical and legal practice, a proprietary model is one whose access and use are governed by restrictive terms that keep one or more core components under provider control. Those components may include the trained weights, source code, architecture details, training data provenance, system prompts, fine-tuning methods, deployment stack or rights to copy, modify, self-host and redistribute. Users may interact through an API, application or licensed package, but they often cannot fully inspect the artefact, reproduce the training pipeline, run independent variants or transfer the model freely across environments. The exact boundary varies, which is why people sometimes distinguish closed-weight, closed-source and proprietary as related but not identical labels.

keyTakeaway: With a proprietary model, you may get the outputs and the service, but much of the model itself stays under the provider’s rules and control.

quickCheck.question: Which statement best describes a proprietary model?
options: It always runs only on the internet and never on local systems.
It can be used through a service or licence while key parts such as weights, code or rights remain under provider control.
It is any model that costs money to access.
It is the same thing as an open-weight model.
quickCheck.explanation: The defining feature is control, not price or where the model runs. Some proprietary models are offered through APIs, some through licensed deployments, but in both cases important technical parts or usage rights remain closed or restricted.

contested: The boundary of "proprietary model" is not fully settled. Some people use it broadly for any commercially restricted AI system, while others distinguish more carefully between closed weights, closed source, restricted licences and hosted-only access.
